entries.topic: The Basel Program and the First Zionist Congress, 1897

claims.text: The Basel Program's aim, in a standard English translation, reads: 'Zionism seeks to establish a home in Palestine for the Jewish people, secured under public law.'

Another published translation renders the aim as 'the establishment of a publicly and legally secured home in Palestine for the Jewish people'; the German original uses the word 'Heimstätte' (home), not 'Staat' (state).

The program named four means: promoting settlement of Jewish agriculturists, artisans and tradesmen in Palestine; organizing all Jews through local and general institutions 'according to the laws of the various countries'; strengthening Jewish national feeling and consciousness; and preparatory steps toward the government consent needed to reach the aim.
The program was adopted unanimously on 30 August 1897 at the First Zionist Congress, which met in Basel from 29 to 31 August 1897.

According to one reference account, the draft first read 'rechtlich' (legally) secured and was changed during the Congress to 'öffentlich-rechtlich' (secured under public law); the reason for the change is not given there.

The Posen Library describes the Congress as attended by some two hundred delegates from seventeen countries; it founded the Zionist Organization, with the Basel Program as its platform, and elected Herzl president.

On 5 June 1897 a notice in the Münchner Neueste Nachrichten rejected holding Herzl's congress in Munich, and in mid-June 1897 (letters dated 13 June) the board of the Munich Jewish congregation wrote to Herzl rejecting it.

On 6 July 1897 the board of the Allgemeiner Rabbiner-Verband (Union of Rabbis in Germany) published a resolution protesting Zionism, citing loyalty to the state and religious messianism; Herzl called these critics 'protest rabbis' (Protestrabbiner).

The Union's declaration, printed in English in the Jewish Chronicle on 9 July 1897 (p. 9), was signed by its executive committee: Maybaum (Berlin), Horovitz (Frankfurt), Guttmann (Breslau), Auerbach (Halberstadt) and Werner (Munich). It called Zionist state efforts 'antagonistic to the messianic promises of Judaism', urged Jews to 'hold aloof' from the movement and its Congress, and did not object to Jewish agricultural colonization of Palestine.
Britain's Orthodox Chief Rabbi Hermann Adler sided with the German rabbis and called Herzl's plan 'völlig unheilbringend' (completely disastrous).
At the Second Zionist Congress in 1898 Herzl's watchword was to 'conquer the communities' (the congregations).

Historian Steven Beller, reviewing Derek Penslar's biography of Herzl (2020), notes that Dreyfus 'is not mentioned by name in the Zionist diary of 1895', and uses this to question the account that the Dreyfus Affair was Herzl's catalyst.

disputes.question: How many delegates, from how many countries, attended the First Zionist Congress?

positions.view: Some two hundred delegates from seventeen countries.
'Some 200 participants' (number of countries not given).
Delegates came from fourteen states.

disputes.question: Was the Dreyfus Affair Herzl's catalyst?

positions.view: Questioned: Dreyfus is not named in Herzl's 1895 Zionist diary (Beller, reviewing Penslar).

claims.text: The Second Congress (Basel, 1898) laid the groundwork for the Jewish Colonial Trust.
The Third Congress (Basel, 1899) resolved that the Jewish Colonial Trust's funds could be spent only in Palestine or Syria.
The Fourth Congress met in London in 1900; religious Zionists led by Yitzhak Ya'akov Reines urged a purely political focus.

The Fifth Congress (Basel, 1901) established the Jewish National Fund; the Democratic Faction (Leo Motzkin, Martin Buber, Chaim Weizmann) pressed for Hebrew culture and more internal democracy; the Congress moved to meeting every other year.
The Sixth Congress (Basel, 1903) voted '295 in favor, 178 against and 98 abstentions' to send a commission to examine settlement in East Africa.
The Seventh Congress (Basel, 1905) voted against a national home outside Palestine and its vicinity; Zangwill's Territorialists walked out; David Wolffsohn became president.

The Eighth Congress (The Hague, 1907) debated 'practical' against 'political' Zionism and supported practical work, including a Palestine branch of the organization under Arthur Ruppin; Weizmann's 'synthetic Zionism' gained ground.
At the Ninth Congress (Hamburg, 1909) the practical camp challenged Wolffsohn's leadership.
At the Tenth Congress (Basel, 1911) the first session was held in Hebrew and the botanist Otto Warburg succeeded Wolffsohn as president.
The Eleventh Congress (Vienna, 1913) backed the founding of a Hebrew University in Jerusalem, which opened twelve years later.

entries.topic: Herzl, Zangwill and the Arab population: the diary, the Khalidi letter and Altneuland, 1895–1905

claims.text: A passage from Herzl's diary of June 1895, as quoted by the Israeli researcher Shaul Arieli (via Edward Said), reads: 'We shall try to spirit the penniless population across the border by procuring employment for it in the transit countries, while denying it any employment in our country.'
Arieli's 2025 survey presents the idea of moving the Arab population as a long-standing strand of Zionist strategic thinking, beginning with this 1895 entry.

Steven Beller, reviewing Derek Penslar's 2020 biography, writes that Herzl was 'quite prepared to remove any local population', though he preferred to do so peacefully, and that 'the context in which he was discussing this was not Palestine' but South America.
Beller also writes that Herzl 'lacked a realistic view about the antagonistic effect' a Jewish settlement would have on the local Arab population, a point Ahad Ha'am raised at the time.
Yusuf Diya al-Khalidi served as mayor of Jerusalem in 1870–76, 1878–79 and 1899–1906, sat for Jerusalem in the first Ottoman parliament, and had taught at the Oriental Academy in Vienna.

On 1 March 1899 al-Khalidi wrote to Zadoc Kahn, chief rabbi of France, for transmission to Herzl. He called the Zionist idea in itself 'natural, beautiful and just', but warned that Palestine was part of the Ottoman Empire and inhabited by others, and wrote: 'in the name of God, let Palestine be left alone.'

Herzl replied on 19 March 1899 that Jewish immigration would benefit the existing population: 'It is their well-being, their individual wealth, which we will increase by bringing in our own.' He asked: 'who would think of sending them away?'
The historian Rashid Khalidi, a descendant of the family, calls the reply condescending and argues it did not answer the central objection that the population would not accept displacement.

Herzl's novel Altneuland (German, 1902) imagines Palestine in 1923 run by a cooperative 'New Society' with public ownership of land; its only Arab character, Reschid Bey, says Arabs had no reason to oppose Jewish immigration because the newcomers 'developed the country and raised everybody's standard of living.'

In 1905 Israel Zangwill, as quoted by Arieli, wrote that 'Palestine itself is already occupied' and that Zionists must be prepared either 'to drive out by the sword the tribes in possession as our forefathers did' or 'to grapple with the problem of a large alien population, mostly Mohammedan and accustomed to despise us.'

disputes.question: What does Herzl's June 1895 diary passage about 'spiriting' the poor population across the border show?

positions.view: An early statement of the transfer idea that ran through Zionist strategic thinking (Arieli).
Herzl was prepared to remove a local population but preferred peaceful means, and the passage was written about South America, not Palestine (Beller on Penslar).

disputes.question: How should Herzl's 1899 reply to al-Khalidi be read?

positions.view: As Herzl framed it: immigration would enrich the existing population, and no one would think of sending them away.
As condescending and evasive: it ignored the warning that the population would not accept displacement (Rashid Khalidi).

claims.text: The Mutasarrifate (Sanjak) of Jerusalem was created as an independent Ottoman administrative unit in 1872, comprising the districts of Jerusalem, Jaffa, Hebron, Beersheba and Gaza; the sanjaks of Nablus and Acre lay to its north. It was dissolved when Britain occupied Palestine in December 1917.
Estimates for about 1890 differ: Roberto Bachi's reconstruction gives 532,000 people (43,000 Jews); the Ottoman census of 1890–91 gives 516,000 (18,000 Jews).
For 1914 Bachi's figures give 689,000 people: 525,000 Muslims, 70,000 Christians and 94,000 Jews. The Ottoman census of 1914–15 gives 722,000: 602,000 Muslims, 81,000 Christians and 39,000 Jews.

Justin McCarthy's adjusted Ottoman figure for 1914–15 is 722,143. The Ottoman register recorded 38,754 Jews, apparently counting only Ottoman subjects; McCarthy puts the true Jewish figure, including foreign nationals, closer to 60,000, against a commonly accepted figure of 85,000 (as summarized by Roger Owen).
McCarthy corrects Ottoman registers chiefly for the undercounting of young children, especially girls, and for missing categories.

The Interactive Encyclopedia of the Palestine Question puts Palestine's Jews at about 60,000 at the start of the war in 1914, 39,000 of them Ottoman citizens, against more than 700,000 Muslim and Christian Ottoman subjects.
The same source counts about 25,000 Jewish immigrants in 1882–1903 and more than 84,000 Jewish immigrants in 1850–1914, not all of whom stayed.
McCarthy re-estimates the 1922 population at 823,684 against the official census total, arguing modern methods correct the census undercount.

disputes.question: How many Jews lived in Palestine in 1914?

positions.view: About 39,000 (38,754): the Ottoman register, which counted Ottoman subjects only.
About 60,000, including foreign nationals (McCarthy; the Palestine Question encyclopedia).
About 85,000, the long-standard figure (as noted by Owen), or 94,000 in Bachi's reconstruction.

disputes.question: How far did the Jewish population fall during the war?

positions.view: About a third left Palestine during 1914–18.
Much less than the commonly cited quarter; many who fled to Alexandria returned (McCarthy).

entries.topic: The Old Yishuv: the Jewish communities already in Palestine

claims.text: The Jewish population of the Land of Israel grew from about 7,000 in 1800 to about 27,000 in 1880, according to the National Library of Israel.
The Old Yishuv was concentrated in the four holy cities of Jerusalem, Hebron, Safed and Tiberias; in the nineteenth century most of it lived in Jerusalem.
It depended almost completely on the halukka, funds from diaspora donors distributed through kollels organized by country of origin and Hasidic affiliation.

The Sephardi chief rabbi (the Hakham Bashi, later titled Rishon LeZion) represented the Jews before the Ottoman authorities; at the end of the nineteenth century the Ashkenazi kollels united under the General Committee of Knesset Israel.
The National Library of Israel describes the First Aliyah, from 1881, as the beginning of a New Yishuv that cost the Old Yishuv its leading position among the Jews of the country.

entries.topic: Kishinev, mass emigration, and the East Africa vote, 1903–1905

claims.text: The Kishinev pogrom took place at Easter, 6–7 April 1903: 49 Jews were killed and more than 500 injured; 700 houses were looted and destroyed and 600 businesses and shops looted; about 2,000 families were left homeless; losses were put at 2,500,000 gold rubles.

P. Krushevan's newspaper Bessarabets had incited the population with a steady stream of articles, including a blood libel. According to the Encyclopaedia Judaica, local and central officials prepared the pogrom, 'evidently with the backing of the minister of the interior, V. Plehve', and the garrison of 5,000 soldiers did not intervene.

Protest meetings were held in London, Paris and New York; a US protest petition handed to President Theodore Roosevelt for the tsar was refused by the tsar. Bialik's poem 'In the Town of Death' answered the pogrom.
A second Kishinev riot in October 1905 killed 19 Jews and injured 56; some Jewish youth formed self-defence units.

Between 1881 and 1914 more than 2.5 million Jews left Eastern Europe, about 80,000 a year: about 2 million went to the United States, about 350,000 to Western Europe, and about 300,000 to other overseas countries, Palestine among them (Shmuel Ettinger).
The Sixth Zionist Congress opened in Basel on 23 August 1903 with about 600 delegates, then the largest; it was the last Congress Herzl chaired.
In his opening address Herzl said of the East Africa offer that 'Zion this certainly is not and can never become', describing it as only an auxiliary colonizing measure.
The Congress voted 295 in favor, 178 against, with 98 abstentions, to send a commission to East Africa; members of the Russian delegation then walked out, arguing the plan violated the Basel Program.
The Seventh Congress in 1905 rejected a national home outside Palestine and its vicinity.

entries.topic: For and against: Reform, Mizrachi, the Democratic Faction, Agudat Israel and German anti-Zionism, 1885–1914

claims.text: The Reform movement's Pittsburgh Platform (1885) declared: 'We consider ourselves no longer a nation but a religious community, and therefore expect neither a return to Palestine' nor the restoration of a Jewish state's laws.

In 1897 the Central Conference of American Rabbis resolved: 'We reaffirm that the object of Judaism is not political nor national, but spiritual.' Isaac Mayer Wise called Judaism 'not tied down to a piece of land here or there.'
The Fifth Zionist Congress (December 1901) declared cultural work an essential part of Zionism.

Mizrachi, the religious-Zionist faction within the Zionist Organization, was founded at a convention in Vilna on 4–5 March 1902 convened by Rabbi Isaac Jacob Reines; Grill counts 72 delegates, 24 of them rabbis.

Mizrachi built 210 branches in the Russian Empire in its first year; its first world conference, at Pressburg on 21–23 August 1904, had about 100 delegates. Its motto was 'The Land of Israel for the people of Israel according to the Torah of Israel.'

When the Tenth Zionist Congress (Basel, 1911) added cultural work to the organization's program, all Mizrachi delegates walked out; a later conference decided not to leave the Zionist Organization, and some leaders who disagreed broke away.

Orthodox opponents in the Frankfurt-based Free Association declared Mizrachi principles incompatible with traditional Judaism in 1902–03; a 1903 pamphlet by Raphael Breuer was titled 'Nationaljudenthum ein Wahnjudenthum!'
Agudat Israel was founded at Kattowitz in late May 1912 as a worldwide association of Torah-observant Jews, largely as a countermeasure to Mizrachi.

In October 1912 liberal German Jews founded a league to combat Zionism, soon renamed the Antizionistisches Komitee; its first pamphlet (early 1913) reached about 45,000 copies by July 1913, an appeal of 1913 carried about 300 signatures, and its declaration appeared in the Berliner Tageblatt on 5 February 1914. Before the war it reportedly had more than 1,000 members.
About twelve days after the Balfour Declaration, in November 1917, anti-Zionist British Jews formed the League of British Jews.

entries.topic: The Second Aliyah, the labor settlements and Hashomer, 1904–1914

claims.text: The National Library of Israel puts the Second Aliyah (1904 to the outbreak of war) at about 35,000 immigrants, mostly from Eastern Europe with a minority from Yemen; the Jewish Virtual Library gives 40,000.
At least half, by the NLI's estimate (nearly half, by the JVL's), left within a few years because of economic hardship; the Jewish community numbered about 80,000 at the end of the period.
The Hebrew Gymnasium, the first Hebrew high school, was founded in Jaffa in 1905 (later the Herzliya Gymnasium).
The idea of Ahuzat Bayit arose in summer 1906; its plots were raffled at Passover 1909 among 60 founding families, and the neighborhood took the name Tel Aviv by majority vote.

Kinneret Farm (1908) was the first Zionist instructional farm; the Merhavia cooperative (1911) disbanded in 1918; a women's training farm founded in 1911 trained about 70 young women before closing in 1917.
The NLI notes that the ideal of 'Hebrew labor' met friction in practice, as many Jewish farmers continued to employ Arab workers.

Bar-Giora was founded in 1907 at Yitzhak Ben-Zvi's home in Neve Tzedek and set up the first Jewish guards' commune at Sejera; Hashomer grew out of it in 1909, led by Yisrael Shohat, and existed until 1920.
Hashomer replaced Arab night watchmen, whom the account describes as colluding with thieves, and made it a condition of guarding a settlement that only Jewish laborers be employed there.

Degania, counted as the first kibbutz, was founded on 28 October 1910 when the 'Hadera Commune' of ten men and two women leased land at Umm Juni from the Jewish National Fund; an earlier group placed there by Ruppin in 1909 had dispersed. The Jewish Virtual Library dates Degania to 1909.

David Ben-Gurion (born David Green in Płońsk, 16 October 1886) landed at Jaffa on 9 September 1906 and went that evening to work in Petah Tikva; he joined the leadership of Poalei Zion, studied law in Istanbul from 1912 with Ben-Zvi, and was expelled by the Ottomans in 1915, going to Alexandria and then New York. Another educational source gives his arrival as 7 September 1907.

Gershon Shafir's study (1989), as summarized by Joel Beinin, argues that First Aliyah colonies relied on cheap Arab labor; that Second Aliyah workers' 'conquest of labor' failed to exclude Arab workers but split the labor market; that planters brought in Yemenite Jews 'who were to be paid Arab wages'; and that the kibbutz and Hashomer were forged in conflict over land and labor rather than mainly by prior ideology.
Against such readings, Anita Shapira argues (as summarized by Rebecca Stein) that the early socialist settlers became conquerors reluctantly, out of 'good will and purity of faith'.

The Jewish Colonization Association, founded by Baron de Hirsch in September 1891 with capital of £2,000,000, took over management of Edmond de Rothschild's Palestine colonies; the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia dates this 'since 1899'.

claims.text: From 1881 to 1882 a few hundred Jews left Sanaa and nearby settlements for Palestine; migration from Yemen continued almost without interruption until 1914, and about 10% of Yemen's Jews left in that period.
In 1884 Yemenite families settled in a new neighborhood, Kfar Hashiloach, in Silwan outside Jerusalem's walls.
In 1911 Shmuel Yavne'eli went to Yemen, at his own request, for the Palestine Office of the Zionist Organization, to encourage immigration; his journey lasted more than a year.
Yavne'eli returned in April 1912; about 1,000 Jews left central and southern Yemen as a result of his efforts, with several hundred more arriving before 1914 (Simon, Laskier and Reguer, 2003).

The National Library of Israel calls the 1911–12 Yemenite immigration 'the first planned immigration operation in the history of Zionism' and counts about 2,000 Yemenite immigrants in the Second Aliyah, about half sent to farming settlements.
Writing in 1913, Yavne'eli reported that over the past year 'some two hundred and fifty to three hundred Yemenite families have settled in the colonies.'

A group of Yemenite families from Sharab reached the Kinneret area in spring 1912 and cleared and farmed land there; according to the Yemenite heritage site Wysinfo, which reproduces the group's letters, disputes with the neighboring Kvutzat Kinneret over land ended in 1930 with the Yemenites' removal to Marmorek, near Rehovot.

entries.topic: Arab responses to Zionism before 1914: Azouri, al-Karmil, the Ottoman parliament, Paris 1913

claims.text: In Le Réveil de la nation arabe (1905), Negib Azouri wrote of the Arab and Jewish national movements: 'Both these movements are destined to fight each other continually until one of them wins.'
Najib Nassar began writing against Zionism in 1905 in al-Muqattam (Cairo) and Lisan al-Hal (Beirut), and in 1908 founded al-Karmil in Haifa, a twice-weekly paper.

The Ottoman authorities closed al-Karmil for two months in June 1909; in 1910 the Ministry of Justice ordered Nassar tried on a complaint from the Jewish community alleging incitement, and the court acquitted him.

In October 1911 Nassar collected his articles as a book, Zionism: Its History, Objectives and Importance; in 1913 he called for a non-Zionist national society based in Nablus; in summer 1914 he urged Palestinian youth to press Arab landowners not to sell land to Jews.

Ruhi al-Khalidi was one of three deputies elected for Jerusalem in 1908 after the Young Turk revolution; in 1911, with his fellow deputy Sa'id al-Husayni, he raised Zionism in the Ottoman parliament, stressing that he opposed Jewish immigration, not the residence of Palestine's own Jews.
Ruhi al-Khalidi left an unpublished manuscript, 'Zionism and the Zionist Question', and died of typhoid in Istanbul in 1913 while deputy to the head of parliament.

The Arab Congress met in Paris on 18–23 June 1913 with 25 official delegates and adopted ten resolutions on Arab participation in the central government, Arabic as an official language and administrative decentralization; its resolutions did not address Zionism, and Zionist representatives Victor Jacobson and Sami Hochberg attended unofficially.

entries.topic: Al-Fula and the first Jezreel Valley purchases, 1910, and the Emek totals

claims.text: Ruppin recalled that in February 1910 Yehoshua Hankin concluded an agreement for 9,500 dunams at Fule (al-Ful), later Merhavia; 3,500 dunams were taken over by the Jewish National Fund and the rest by the Palestine Land Development Company.

Ruppin wrote that the Turkish government refused to authorize the sale and that 'the Governor in Nazareth, a rabid anti-Zionist', declared he would fight it; permission was obtained through Hankin's friends in Constantinople.
The district governor (qaimaqam) of Nazareth from 1910 was Shukri al-Asali, who tried and failed to stop Elias Sursuq's sale of about 2,500 acres of al-Fula land.

Al-Asali resigned in 1911 to win a by-election to the Ottoman parliament for Damascus, where he argued that Jewish settlers held Ottoman citizenship alongside foreign citizenship and were taking control of rural villages; he served until April 1912.
Al-Asali was hanged in Marjeh Square, Damascus, on 6 May 1916 by order of Jamal Pasha, among a group of Arab nationalists.

Ruppin wrote that Hankin had first reached agreement in 1891 for 160,000 dunams at 15 francs a dunam; that in 1920 about 70,000 dunams were bought at £3 (unirrigated) and £6.5 (partly irrigated) a dunam, about £300,000 in all; and that by 1929 about 290,000 dunams had been bought in the Emek and the Acre plain since 1910, for £970,000.
Ruppin's account says Hankin 'enjoyed the confidence of the Arabs' and that owners sold because they wanted cash; it does not mention the tenants on the land.

disputes.question: How did the al-Fula sale look to the parties?

positions.view: A willing sale by owners who wanted cash, through a buyer they trusted (Ruppin's 1929 memoir).
A sale the Ottoman district governor tried to block, and which he raised in parliament as a danger to rural villages (al-Asali).

entries.topic: Palestine in the First World War, 1914–1917

claims.text: In December 1914 up to 6,000 Russian citizens, all Jewish, were expelled from Jaffa.
By the end of January 1915 some 7,000 Jewish refugees from Palestine were in British-held Alexandria, according to contemporary New York Times reports cited by a 2021 JNS column.
In 1915 the Ottoman authorities required non-citizens, Jews included, to take Ottoman citizenship or leave; the Zion Mule Corps was formed by the British Army that year from Jews exiled to Egypt.

Locusts swarmed over Palestine, Mount Lebanon and Syria from March to October 1915; the historian Zachary Foster estimates they cut the 1915 winter harvest of wheat and barley by 10–15 per cent and destroyed 60–100 per cent of summer and autumn fruit and vegetables.

The Ottoman authorities required every male aged 15 to 60 in the cities to collect 20 kg of locust eggs or pay a fine (£4.40); the New York Times reported that 800 people had paid the fine by 21 November 1915.

The American University of Beirut's exhibit lists the causes of famine in Greater Syria as the 1915 Allied blockade of the eastern Mediterranean, drought, locusts and Ottoman paper money, and states that Mount Lebanon lost 20–30 per cent of its population.

Djemal (Jamal) Pasha ordered the evacuation of Jaffa on 28 March 1917; the deportation took place on 6 April 1917. Estimates of those displaced range from about 10,000, including 8,000 Jews, to up to 16,000 from Tel Aviv.

Muslim residents of Jaffa were able to return soon after; the Jewish deportees could not return until summer 1918. About 1,500 are thought to have died as a result of the deportation, though the deaths were not properly recorded.
A US consular report published in the New York Times on 3 June 1917 described looting and killings of deportees; these reports are cited by the JNS column.
